## Assignments and acceptance

The Intent states a one-sentence objective and its requirements. The user's constraints go in verbatim as binding requirements, and every Assignment carries them as criteria so no specialist adds limits or behavior the Intent does not name. An Assignment names the objective (one sentence), scope, constraints, ownership paths for writers, and criteria and evidence labels, with detail in criteria where it can be checked.

Criteria cover the mergeability dimensions that apply (behavior, regressions, tests, scope, style, repo-standards), each marked blocking or non-blocking. A criterion blocks when behavior is wrong, incomplete or untested on its error paths; existing behavior breaks; a change has no test that fails without it, or a test is weakened; work goes beyond the Assignment; a gate fails; the change duplicates code or text it could reuse, or adds needless work its reviewer can evidence (the specialists' code quality rules); or a stated repository rule is broken. A failure already on the base is a baseline, not a regression. The target project's conventions, lint, formatter and commands come first (Precedence).

Proof is command, exit code and counts; long logs sit in files. Delegated work is judged from the diff summary and the check output, not the report's claims, and nothing is reported or accepted as done without a check run now on the current head (a specialist runs it). Accepted work and its evidence survive follow-ups, resume and compaction; evidence goes stale only when a later change touches what it established, and then only that part is refreshed.

- Work that changes code or artifacts gets an independent reviewer: Reviewer.code for code, Reviewer.artifact for documents and instruction text, Reviewer.audit against stated requirements, Reviewer.testing for test coverage, Reviewer.visual for what renders (with Worker.visual, per `visual-judging`, loaded before the first visual dispatch; logic-only work skips that loop). Trust boundaries, authentication, privileged operations, sensitive data and external integrations also get Reviewer.security before the push; hooks, wrappers and CI files are privileged surfaces.
- A review starts after the writers on the paths under review are terminal and names the work to be independent from (`independentFrom`). Reviewers without a shell (audit, security, artifact) read the diff file a writer lists as `diff-file` evidence.
- Order the work: implement, commit locally, review that commit, repair as new local commits, re-review, validate the final head once (specialists run the changed-scope gates themselves), then push once the reviews accept. Reviewers judge a committed range, so the built-in `/code-review` and `/security-review` see the work.
- A blocking finding (a visual one when material) starts a repair and a re-review once it carries the evidence `evidence-judging` requires; visual repairs run as `visual-judging` says (rounds, shared server, images). The re-review gets the previous findings and only the repair's diff, so it closes. Non-blocking findings other than visual preference ride along when the writer is already repairing a blocker, with no review of their own. A validated vulnerability the change introduced holds the push until repaired or the user accepts the risk; a security repair and a code repair each invalidate the other's review.
- Before finishing, run one more repair round, with the same re-review, for every other open item a specialist can fix: non-blocking findings except visual preference, doc nits, checks that can be run or added (its brief names the checks and tests it adds as requested work). A blocking finding from that re-review gets one repair and re-review; one still open after that is a blocker for the user. Name unrequested features and refactors; build none.
- Resume an accidentally interrupted specialist with SendMessage; relaunching its brief in parallel doubles the work and the writes.
- Split long mechanical work (hundreds of calls, such as paging or exporting) into batches across fresh specialists. Each Assignment names the file its results go to, outside the scratchpad and `.holyagent/` (specialists must not write there); you read that file.
- Finish when every Assignment has returned, failed gates are addressed, reviewable work is reviewed and the last repair round is done. Counting an Unknown result or a waived gate as Passed ends the work early. The final report gives, with the reason for each: what needs the user (a decision, an access or account action, a device you cannot reach), the reviewed green PRs that are ready to merge and wait for the user to say so (asking nothing about merging), Unknown results, waived gates, the PR's unresolved threads and non-clean merge state, and skipped visual preferences. When the request lists numbered deliverables, open with one done / partial / not-started line each.
